title: Patagonia
description: Argentina's southern frontier: wind, latitude and fresher Pinot Noir and Malbec.
L: Patagonia's wine regions lie in southern Argentina, mainly in Neuquén and Río Negro, around 38 to 39 degrees south, with smaller plantings further south in Chubut, near 43 to 45 degrees. Vineyards are low, about 300 m, in river valleys. It has about 3,500 hectares, a small share of Argentina's total.

Unlike Mendoza and Salta, Patagonia is cool because of latitude, not altitude. Summers are sunny with long days, nights are cold, and strong, constant winds blow from the west. The wind keeps grapes healthy, reduces disease and thickens skins. Rainfall is low; irrigation comes from the Limay, Neuquén and Río Negro rivers.
What makes Patagonia cool, unlike Mendoza?

Río Negro has grown grapes since the early 20th century, with some old vines, like Malbec and Sémillon planted in the 1930s and 1940s. Neuquén's vineyards were mostly planted from the early 2000s, in the desert, with modern irrigation. Producers like Bodega Chacra, Noemía and Familia Schroeder show its potential.

Patagonia is Argentina's best region for Pinot Noir. Its cool climate and long, sunny days give red cherry, raspberry and spice, with fresh acidity and fine tannins. Old Pinot Noir vines in Río Negro, like those at Bodega Chacra, planted in 1932 and 1955, make some of South America's most acclaimed Pinots.

Patagonian Malbec is fresher and more elegant than Mendoza's, with red fruit, violet and brighter acidity. Merlot, Cabernet Franc and Sauvignon Blanc also do well. Old Sémillon in Río Negro gives textured whites. Chubut, further south, grows Chardonnay and Pinot Noir for sparkling and still wines.

Patagonia's grapes are fresher than in the north.
Try a Patagonian Malbec next to a Mendoza one. The southern wine is usually lighter, fresher and redder in fruit.
Which grape makes some of South America's most acclaimed wines in Río Negro?
Old-vine Pinot Noir, like Bodega Chacra's.

Reading Patagonia and eating with it

Labels show the grape and the region: Patagonia, Neuquén, Río Negro or Chubut. Some note the latitude, like 45 degrees south, as a selling point, as altitude is in the north. Argentina's 85% rule applies.

Patagonian Pinot Noir suits lamb, Patagonian lamb roasted al asador, trout from Andean lakes, salmon and mushrooms. Malbec suits beef and game. Sémillon suits fish and poultry. Serve Pinot at 14 to 16 degrees, Malbec at 16 to 18.

Patagonian lamb is a regional speciality.
Patagonian lamb is slow-roasted on an iron cross over an open fire, al asador, a perfect match for fresh Pinot or Malbec.
Patagonian Pinot Noir suits trout and salmon.
Yes. Its freshness and low tannin suit fish.
